cases.abstract: FlashAttention-2 addresses GPU execution costs that remain after tiled attention eliminates quadratic intermediate matrices from high-bandwidth memory. Repeated normalization is expensive relative to matrix multiplication, and limited parallelism or exchanges of partial outputs between warps can still constrain throughput. The method postpones normalization until the output is complete, distributes query blocks across multiprocessors when batches and head counts provide too little parallel work, and assigns query rows to warps to avoid cross-warp output reductions. It preserves exact attention with auxiliary memory linear in sequence length. Across the tested A100 attention configurations, FlashAttention-2 is 1.7-3.0 times faster than FlashAttention and 3-10 times faster than standard PyTorch attention. Training 1.3B- and 2.7B-parameter GPT-style models on eight A100 GPUs reaches 225 TFLOPs/s per GPU, with larger gains over FlashAttention at 8k than at 2k contexts. Multi-query decoding instead requires rapid loading of the KV cache: distributing these reads across thread blocks achieves attention-kernel speedups of up to seven times over FasterTransformer on A100. The two workloads therefore require different partitions of work to exploit available GPU capacity.
cases.methods: FlashAttention-2 avoids normalizing the partial attention output after every key/value block, reducing operations that cannot use fast GPU matrix-multiplication units. For each query block, it keeps a running row maximum, an exponential sum, and an unnormalized sum of values weighted by exponentiated attention scores. When a new block raises the maximum, the previous exponential sum and value accumulator are multiplied by exp(old maximum - new maximum) before adding the new contributions. Rescaling places all processed blocks on the same exponential scale; dividing the accumulator by the final sum then produces the full softmax-weighted output. Thus normalization is deferred without approximating attention or materializing the complete score and probability matrices. Saving each row's logsumexp permits probabilities to be recomputed in the backward pass. The algorithm still performs quadratic arithmetic in sequence length, but its additional storage is linear.
cases.results: The end-to-end benefit of FlashAttention-2 depends on context length. In GPT-style training on eight A100 80GB SXM4 GPUs, replacing FlashAttention raises the 1.3B-parameter model's throughput from 189 to 196 TFLOPs/s per GPU at 2k context, but from 170 to 220 at 8k. The 2.7B-parameter model similarly rises from 175 to 225 at 8k. The larger gains at long context are consistent with attention's growing share of computation, rather than a uniform transfer of kernel speedups to full training. The 225 TFLOPs/s peak corresponds to 72% model FLOPs utilization under a convention counting the full causal attention matrix; kernel benchmarks instead halve attention FLOPs for causal masking. Those rates therefore require different accounting conventions. Memory feasibility is a separate benefit: at 16k sequence length, standard PyTorch attention runs out of memory in the kernel tests, while FlashAttention-2 still runs without storing quadratic attention intermediates.
cases.notes: The abstract retains execution overhead and workload-specific partitioning as the contribution, not a new asymptotic reduction. Section 3.1 supports the rescaling explanation; Table 1 supports context-dependent training gains, and Figure 4 supports the PyTorch memory failure. The body states a 2.8-fold training speedup, whereas Table 1's 220 versus 72 implies approximately 3.06-fold; the passages avoid assigning a maximum over the baseline without FlashAttention. Training and kernel FLOPs use different causal-mask conventions. Automatic tuning and H100-specific optimizations remain proposed work.

cases.abstract: Speculative decoding replaces some serial target-model evaluations with concurrent verification while preserving the target's chosen sampling distribution. A cheaper model drafts several tokens, and the target evaluates their conditional probabilities in parallel. Probability-ratio tests retain an accepted prefix; after the first rejection, sampling from the positive residual between target and proposal probabilities restores the target mass not supplied by accepted guesses. This correction works for any proposal model without retraining the target. The latency analysis balances distributional overlap against proposal cost, assuming independent, identically distributed acceptance rates, sufficiently long generations, and spare compute that makes concurrent target evaluations no slower than one ordinary evaluation. In batch-one tests with the 11B-parameter T5-XXL on a single TPU-v4, the 77M-parameter T5-small proposal accelerates English-German translation by 2.6 times under standard sampling and 3.4 times under greedy decoding. Corresponding summarization speedups are 2.3 and 3.1 times. Larger proposals improve acceptance but produce smaller speedups in these tests, so agreement with the target must be weighed against the time spent drafting.
cases.methods: Speculative decoding separates cheap token proposals from exact sampling of the target distribution. For each drafted token x, it uses the acceptance probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), with p and q conditioned on the same prefix and adjusted for the sampling rule. Accepted proposals supply probability mass min(p(x), q(x)); sampling a replacement from the normalized positive part of p - q supplies the remainder. After the first rejection, later drafts are discarded because their conditioning prefix no longer applies. If all gamma guesses pass, a further token is sampled from the target. Each iteration therefore emits between one and gamma + 1 tokens without approximating the target distribution. Under i.i.d. acceptance rates of mean alpha, the expected count is 1 + alpha + ... + alpha^gamma. Dividing by 1 + gamma*c gives predicted speedup for long generations, assuming relative proposal latency c and concurrent verification costing one target step.
cases.results: The fastest tested proposal model is not the one with the highest acceptance rate. In English-German translation with T5-XXL on a single TPU-v4 at batch size one, greedy decoding with seven guesses gives a 3.4-fold speedup using the 77M-parameter T5-small, versus 1.7-fold using the 800M-parameter T5-large, even though mean acceptance rises from 0.75 to 0.82. With draft length fixed, this ordering is consistent with proposal cost offsetting the benefit of greater agreement. For T5-small, standard sampling lowers acceptance to 0.62 and speedup to 2.6-fold at the same seven guesses, so the sampling rule also changes attainable gains. Summarization yields smaller T5-small speedups of 2.3-fold under standard sampling and 3.1-fold under greedy decoding, each using five guesses. These are latency gains, not reductions in arithmetic work: rejected drafts waste computation, and concurrent verification requires spare compute capacity.
cases.notes: The Methods paragraph links accepted probability mass and residual correction to exact sampling; the runtime formula remains conditional. Results use Table 2's translation comparison at fixed gamma = 7 under greedy decoding, making the acceptance-cost tradeoff clearer without treating proposal size as an isolated cause. Walltime measurements cover T5 only; GPT-like and LaMDA results report acceptance rather than speed. Equal output distributions do not imply identical sampled sequences. The sampling comparison concerns transformed distributions, and the latency gains do not establish lower arithmetic cost.
